slides.title: Chapter 6: Geodesics and Distance
slides.notes: Set the agenda by stating that this chapter promotes geodesics from solutions of an ODE to the central tool that controls distance on a Riemannian manifold. Highlight the four pillars: a variational characterization, local minimization in normal neighborhoods, the induced distance function, and a global completeness theorem. Tell students that everything we do today rests on the first variation formula and on a single careful use of the inverse function theorem.

slides.title: Two Functionals on Admissible Curves
slides.notes: Stress that length is what we ultimately care about because it is a geometric invariant of the image of the curve. Energy is the convenience: it is convex in the velocity and produces an ODE without square roots. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality reconciles them and forces constant-speed parametrization on energy minimizers. This is the moment to remind students that the variational problem is the same one Euler studied for shortest paths.

slides.title: The First Variation Yields the Geodesic Equation
slides.notes: Walk through the derivation in three moves: differentiate energy under the integral, swap the order of differentiation using the symmetry lemma, then integrate by parts using metric compatibility. The boundary terms vanish because we fixed endpoints, leaving an integral that must vanish against every admissible variation field. The fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations then forces the covariant acceleration to be zero pointwise. Underscore that this is the same ODE we previously took as a definition; here we earn it from a variational principle.

slides.title: Geodesics Locally Minimize Length
slides.notes: Frame the slide around the slogan: geodesics are local, distance is global. The inverse function theorem applied to the exponential map at the origin gives a radius beyond which the ODE solutions sweep out a diffeomorphic image of a Euclidean ball. Inside that ball every other admissible curve is strictly longer than the radial geodesic. Remind students that minimization can fail beyond the injectivity radius even when the geodesic continues to exist.

slides.title: Uniformly Normal Neighborhoods
slides.notes: Pinpoint the upgrade from normal to uniformly normal. A normal neighborhood lives at a single basepoint; a uniformly normal neighborhood works for every basepoint inside it with one shared radius. This is the technical refinement that lets us patch local minimizers and is the device behind the proof that the distance function is continuous. Mention that compactness of a closed geodesic ball plus continuous dependence of the exponential map are what make the construction possible.

slides.title: The Gauss Lemma: Radial Orthogonality
slides.notes: The Gauss lemma is the geometric statement behind the inequality that makes radial geodesics shortest. Once we know that the radial vector is orthogonal to the geodesic sphere, we can decompose any competing curve into a radial part and a tangential part. The Pythagorean estimate gives a strictly positive transverse cost unless the curve stays radial. Encourage students to read the lemma as a regularity statement about the exponential map: angles at the base point persist outward, at least along the radial direction.

slides.title: The Riemannian Distance Generates the Topology
slides.notes: Underline that the distance function is not a new structure layered on top of the manifold; it is the metric that the smooth and Riemannian data already determine. Each metric axiom reduces to a concrete local fact: the Gauss lemma supplies the separation property and the uniformly normal neighborhoods supply the basis comparison. The students should leave the slide convinced that geodesic balls really are the basic open sets for the original topology.

slides.title: Hopf-Rinow: Equivalent Completeness Statements
slides.notes: Hopf-Rinow is the central global theorem of the chapter. State the four equivalents carefully so students see that two are metric, one is dynamical, and one is analytic. The proof proceeds by extension: starting at the supremum of times for which a minimizer exists, use the uniformly normal neighborhood at the limit point to extend it. The counter-example with a puncture shows that completeness is not automatic and that bounded sets can fail to be compact without it.

slides.title: Semigeodesic Coordinates as a Distance Tool
slides.notes: Position semigeodesic coordinates, also called Fermi coordinates, as the natural successor to normal coordinates. Where normal coordinates radiate from a point, semigeodesic coordinates radiate from a hypersurface. The metric block decomposes because the radial direction is orthogonal to the transverse one by the Gauss lemma applied along the hypersurface. The payoff is operational: many distance and curvature computations near a hypersurface reduce to ODEs in the radial variable.

slides.title: What This Chapter Hands Forward
slides.notes: Close by re-emphasizing the three altitudes: variational, local, global. Each later chapter on Jacobi fields, comparison theorems, or curvature bounds will rely on one of these three readings of a geodesic. Encourage students to keep a mental flowchart: ODE for existence, normal ball for minimization, Hopf-Rinow for global statements, semigeodesic coordinates for distance computations near submanifolds.
